name: Exilis Ultra / Exilis Elite

lead: Exilis is a BTL radiofrequency machine used in clinics for non-surgical skin tightening and body contouring on the face and body. Ultra and Elite are newer versions of the platform. Wikipedia lists it among commercial RF skin-tightening devices.

RF current is converted to heat in the skin, with the aim of contracting collagen and prompting new collagen over months, tightening lax skin and fine lines. RF devices are described as an alternative to facelifts and other surgery, used on jowls, abdomen, thighs and arms. The sources reviewed describe the RF category in general; model-specific trial data were not found.

paras: Clinicians deliver it in a series of in-office sessions with little downtime. Results build over months.
Category reports include redness, swelling, pain, burns, blistering, pigment change and, less commonly, scarring or fat loss. Pacemakers and pregnancy are listed contraindications.

angle.text: Exilis is used for non-surgical tightening of the face and body. Radiofrequency heats the skin, contracting collagen and prompting new collagen over months. Sources reviewed describe the RF category more than this device specifically.

lead: Exilis is a line of in-office radiofrequency (RF) devices made by BTL for non-surgical skin tightening and body contouring; Exilis Elite is the older RF-only version and Exilis Ultra 360 is the later version that adds ultrasound to the same handpiece, according to clinic descriptions.[1][2] People have it done on the face, neck and body to firm lax skin, soften the look of jowls and fine lines, and reduce small pockets of fat without surgery.[1][3]

RF skin tightening in general passes radiofrequency energy into the skin, where it becomes heat in the dermis. Proponents say this stimulates collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production and so tightens tissue over the following months; Wikipedia presents RF devices as a non-surgical alternative to facelifts and other surgery.[1][3]

Published work specific to Exilis consists mainly of small studies on the platform's focused monopolar RF: a 30-person prospective facial study, a labial-laxity cohort and two pig studies on collagen and fat-cell effects.[4][5][6][7]

paras: Wikipedia lists Exilis as BTL's entry among RF skin-tightening devices, alongside systems from Solta, Venus Concept, Syneron, Lutronic, Lumenis and DEKA.[1] RF devices heat the dermis to induce remodeling; Wikipedia cites an ideal dermal target temperature of 67 degrees C and notes that cooling can be adjusted so the energy also heats and reduces fat.[1]

According to a UK clinic's description, Exilis Ultra 360 delivers monopolar RF and ultrasound at the same time through one handpiece: the RF does the heating, and the ultrasound is said to help the heat spread evenly and reach deeper. Built-in cooling protects the skin surface while tissue beneath is held at roughly 40 to 42 degrees C, a range the clinic says causes existing collagen fibres to contract and fat cells to begin breaking down, with fat cells damaged by the heat cleared by the lymphatic system over the following weeks [2]. The Elite model is described there as the older, RF-only version [2].

Wikipedia's account of RF skin tightening lists many competing systems and says the penetration depth of the energy depends on electrode configuration (monopolar, bipolar or unipolar), with microneedle RF devices forming a separate group [1].

Wikipedia describes RF devices as used on jowls, abdomen, thighs and arms, and for cellulite and body contouring.[1] In a 2022 prospective study of 30 adults aged 25 to 65, three weekly sessions of monopolar RF were reported to improve temporal and malar fat loss, periorbital hollowing and puffiness on a facial grading scale.[4]
Focused monopolar RF has also been studied for labial laxity, where four treatments at weekly intervals improved vulvar appearance scores in 17 women.[6]

Grokipedia summarizes category-wide reports of modest immediate tightening that increases over three to six months, and notes that many RF studies are small and lack randomized controls.[3] Wikipedia reports pain requiring sedation in some patients, skin dents from uneven healing, and fat necrosis or atrophic scarring with RF devices.[1] Grokipedia lists redness, swelling, burns, blistering and hyperpigmentation among reported effects, and pacemakers and pregnancy as contraindications.[3]
In the labial study, no adverse events were reported and 94% of participants described mild or no discomfort.[6]

A 2022 prospective study of 30 subjects found that three weekly monopolar RF sessions improved all measured parameters on a facial grading scale, with statistically significant improvement for grade-4 temporal and malar fat loss, periorbital hollowing and puffiness.[4] A 2016 prospective cohort of 17 women reported improved vulvar appearance and an 18% rise in total FSFI score after four sessions.[6]

Animal work includes a 2015 pig study in which weekly treatments for four weeks raised skin collagen content from about 9.0% to 25.9% at three months, and a 2014 pig study in which the apoptotic index of subcutaneous fat cells rose from 7% to 40-53% with the skin surface intact; these are animal data.[5][7]

The UK clinic describes a course as four to six sessions one to two weeks apart, with facial sessions lasting 30 to 45 minutes and body sessions about the same per area. It says some firmness may be visible after the first session, the main change appears from about four weeks, results keep improving for a couple of months after the course, and most people's results last around a year before a top-up course is suggested [2]. The sensation is described as warm, sometimes briefly hot, with skin staying pink for about an hour [2]. The studies cited here used three to four weekly sessions [4][6].

The same clinic says the treatment suits loose or crepey skin over a soft layer of fat and cellulite, and that firm fat pockets or heavy sagging are better matched to other approaches such as fat freezing, HIFU or surgery [2]. This page is promotional clinic content that does not cite the studies it refers to [2].

Contraindications listed by the clinic include pregnancy, metal implants or a pacemaker and active skin infection in the treatment area [2], consistent with the contraindications Grokipedia lists for RF devices in general [3].

Exilis is sold to clinics, and treatment is offered at aesthetic and medical-spa practices that describe it as an FDA-cleared device for non-invasive skin tightening and body contouring; the exact clearance wording varies between clinic descriptions and was not checked against the FDA's 510(k) database here. RF tightening more generally is positioned as a lower-downtime option between topical products and surgical facelifts [1]. In appearance-focused communities, in-office RF is discussed alongside HIFU, microneedling RF and other non-surgical tightening procedures.
